contentHtml:
India’s nutrition landscape is undergoing a significant shift, with undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies and rising obesity presenting a complex public health challenge. At the same time, the growing popularity of quick-fix diets, protein supplements and gut-health products has raised concerns about misinformation and the commercialisation of nutrition.

In an interaction with ETHealthworld, Dr Sarath Gopalan, President, Nutrition Society of India, discusses India's triple burden of malnutrition, the need for evidence-based nutrition communication, the role of personalised nutrition and AI, and the growing concerns around childhood nutrition and dietary habits.

Advt

1. India's nutrition landscape is undergoing a significant transition, with undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies coexisting with rising obesity and metabolic disorders. How would you assess India's progress in addressing this burden? Are our current nutrition policies and interventions keeping pace with changing dietary patterns and health needs?

Over the past 35 years, we have moved from solely undernutrition to overnutrition. And after 2010 a third dimension was added: a person can be well nourished, or even overnourished, and still have micronutrient deficiencies. India now faces a triple burden of nutrition.

A one-size-fits-all policy will not work. The Dietary Guidelines for Indians, released by the ICMR-NIN in 2024, offer a general guideline for the community, but we also need a personalised approach, to a particular individual in specific situations.

At the same time, we must keep pace with evolving scientific evidence and ensure that our messaging remains accurate. Institutions should work closely with media professionals across television, radio, print and social media. Take the example of ORS and polio. Every family knows what ORS is and the importance of Polio vaccination. Similarly, our nutrition-related messaging should focus on key issues and the importance of physical activity.

Advt

2. There is a growing consumer appetite for quick fixes in nutrition, from crash diets and detox products to supplements promising rapid weight loss, improved gut health and hormonal balance. How big is the gap between evidence-based nutrition and what consumers are being sold?The general tendency is that over a period of years we have become lazy people. At one stage we used to walk up to the TV to switch it on. Now you can lie in your bed and just use the remote. Everything has become mechanized, and we hardly want to exert ourselves. So, if you can sit on a chair and lose two or three kgs, the idea will appeal to you.

Advt

That is where things are wrong, especially in children. At a growing age it's important not to drastically curtail food intake and nutrition intake in a child. Even if a child is overweight or becoming obese, the focus should be more on burning the excess calories through adequate physical exercise.In adults, one can be a little more aggressive in restricting certain foods and nutrients, but even then, exercise is crucial. Burning calories is far healthier than starving or taking quick-fix potions that stop food from being absorbed. When you exercise, your whole body is working, your circulation improves and your cells are better oxygenated, which is a much healthier way of mobilising energy and fat. Quick fixes may make you lose weight immediately, but the moment there is a gap, it comes back.

3. Protein has become one of the biggest nutrition trends in India, with consumers increasingly focusing on protein intake, powders and fortified products. Are we seeing a genuine improvement in nutritional awareness, or is protein being oversimplified as the answer to broader nutritional problems? How should nutritional requirements be assessed rather than following trends?Scientifically, the best diet is a balanced one, with protein being an important component. It is essential for several bodily functions, including muscle and tissue development. However, its growing commercialisation, particularly among young people, creates the impression that consuming large amounts of protein will automatically make them fitter and more muscular.Many teenagers are aware of whey protein and similar supplements but are not adequately informed about the risks of excessive intake. Unrestricted and irresponsible use can be harmful and counterproductive, with very high protein intake potentially placing a severe load on the kidneys over the long term. High-protein diets have a place in the right setting. Sportspersons undertaking strenuous training, for instance, follow planned diets tailored to their requirements, often with guidance from sports nutritionists. This cannot be generalised to every teenager looking to stay healthy.Everything has to be put in perspective. The disproportionate focus on protein can come at the expense of other nutrients, contributing to widespread micronutrient deficiencies among teenagers, particularly iron deficiency in both boys and girls.4. Gut health and the microbiome have emerged as major areas of interest, with probiotics, prebiotics and gut-health supplements gaining popularity. Are consumers increasingly self-diagnosing digestive issues and turning to supplements without understanding the underlying cause?Many people don't even reach healthcare professionals. They take these products at home after seeing advertisements, and they assume that if something is described as good, it is unlikely to do any harm. That may not be the case. They need to think: do we really need it on a long-term basis? And how much of it is actually helping us?My answer is to go by published scientific data, not purely marketed data. People should weigh the evidence available, rather than relying on advertisements in print or on TV and taking supplements without consulting a doctor, dietitian or any other healthcare professional. Check the scientific basis for a particular supplement, how credible the data is and whether it has been well reviewed.Some people feel a supplement is good and keep taking one after another. There is an upper limit, and there is what the body actually needs. Someone may think that taking four or five vitamin D tablets instead of one will leave them better off. Dangerous trends like this start with self-medication, which is a huge problem in India and needs to be addressed effectively. People can self-medicate because they have such easy access to these products. In many European and other countries, you can’t buy medication or supplements over the counter like this. Here, easy access makes people think they can bypass the system, but they are not prepared to deal with any problems that arise.5. Personalised nutrition matters even more in India, where diets vary so widely from region to region. How can we better understand regional nutritional needs, and how can data and AI help us shape policies that reach communities still affected by undernutrition?We already have published, public-domain data on nutrition and micronutrient status across the country, including which states are more deficient in certain micronutrients than others. But India’s population keeps growing, and updating that analysis three or five years later using the same methods would be slow and difficult. The advantage of AI is that it can connect this data very quickly and save a great deal of time. It can give us a general idea of which regions have more obesity, or are more deficient in iron or another nutrient.For example, there are pockets in North India, such as Haryana, where people may be well built but there is a lot of iron deficiency, whereas in the northeast, in places like Manipur, it is the lowest. This comes down to diet. A diet rich in fat and carbohydrates can still fall short on iron, whereas the animal-based foods widely eaten in much of the northeast are very rich sources of iron. We already understand this, but AI would help us reach more places and cover more ground in less time, giving us far more data to build on.Of course, there will be exceptions within any region, so individual counselling by professionals who can design a specific nutritional plan remains important. Both need to go hand in hand. Community-level data tells us the general pattern, much as we know that Europeans are, on average, taller than Indians. If a trend is known for a region, most people there will share it, and anyone who doesn’t fit can be identified and given a personalised approach. It has to be a combination of both.6. Childhood nutrition is facing new challenges, from changing dietary habits and increased screen time to declining physical activity and rising obesity. How are these changes affecting children's growth and cognitive development? Screen time is a big concern, and wherever there is an opportunity, we must project the message about limiting it. Nowhere was this more apparent than in the post-COVID era. During the lockdown, going out was curtailed. To keep children occupied, parents handed them a mobile or a game. Screen time went up significantly, and children did not develop social skills. Multiple schools have told us that the developmental age of a five-year-old after that period was closer to that of a three or three-and-a-half-year-old. Children are slower to grasp, communicate and pick things up, and their mental age is lower, because they have not had the exposure. They also hardly maintain eye contact or talk to each other the way children used to, and this will get worse with more mechanisation.Food is an important conversation. Some schools have become very aggressive, and governments are active too. In Karnataka, for example, foods high in fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) are not allowed within 50 metres of a school, and some school stores serve only healthy options. That is a welcome step. The same should apply in other places, such as cinema halls. That will set an example.7. Micronutrient deficiencies remain widespread in India despite decades of supplementation, fortification and public nutrition programmes. Where are we falling short and what should we change?We need to look critically at where the problem lies. Is it at the implementation level, the supervision level, or somewhere else? Take iron, for example. Anaemia has been a problem for decades, we have had an anaemia control programme running all along, and yet it is still a significant problem.The other important aspect is communication. We already have validated dietary guidelines and resources, including an excellent book of dietary guidelines and recipes brought out by ICMR-NIN. These need to reach a much larger audience through innovative formats such as videos and media campaigns. Nutrition messages must be communicated repeatedly and effectively, just as commercial advertisements for supplements and food products reach consumers every day.For instance, while there is widespread communication around exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, there is far less awareness about the timely introduction of complementary foods after six months. Delayed complementary feeding is an important contributor to nutritional and growth faltering in children. Yet, we hardly see public messages emphasising its importance. Such messages need to feature more prominently on public display boards and media channels.8. As President of the Nutrition Society of India, how do you see the role of scientific institutions and professional bodies evolving amid the growing commercialisation of nutrition? How can the Society help strengthen evidence-based nutrition education, improve public understanding and ensure that emerging research informs clinical practice and public policy?Scientific institutions can serve as go-to bodies for high-quality, validated research and develop stringent protocols to provide practical approaches to specific situations. Professional bodies and societies, such as the Nutrition Society of India, can play a far more effective role in communicating these important nutritional messages.We have several chapters across India, some of which have adopted local villages and are disseminating scientifically accurate nutritional information. The research is already validated; what has been lacking is public awareness. It is important to communicate this information in languages people understand, taking into account their level of education and awareness.As nutrition bodies and professional societies, we can reach communities more effectively through our chapters, media partners and other channels. We are making progress, but we certainly need to step up these efforts and communicate more aggressively.
